newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus sign deal to seek integration.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus sign deal to seek integration.

text.p: Russia and Belarus signed an outline Union Treaty on Wednesday but agreed to rework the details after 11th-hour intervention by liberals in Moscow wary of further integration with Russia's controversial neighbour.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin signed the treaty with Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko.
"The union does not create a single state. Each side maintains its sovereignty. At the same time it takes our integration onto a qualitatively new phase," Yeltsin said after the signing.

The accord was designed to build on a "community treaty" signed exactly a year ago when Yeltsin, then running for re-election, sought to appeal to nostalgia among Russian voters for the Soviet Union which collapsed in 1991.
But it was a far cry from the document backed by Lukashenko, who wants eventually to unite his struggling 10-million-strong former Soviet republic with the vast Russian Federation.

Few people in either country oppose integration, but there is fierce debate in Russia about the wisdom of rushing into a partnership with a country whose poor human rights record and slow reforms have put it on a collision course with the West.
The original 17-page draft was reduced to a three-page statement of intent in furious last-minute bargaining sparked by reformists appointed last month to Russia's new-look cabinet.
"Preparations for the document unfortunately did not take place without bitter opposition," said a grim-faced Lukashenko, barely hiding his disappointment at the signing ceremony.
But Yeltsin appeared to have performed a difficult political balancing act, winning the approval of Russia's opposition communist leader Gennady Zyuganov.
An accompanying charter, containing the meat of the original draft, was merely initialled by the two presidents and sent for six weeks of reworking and public discussion.
Liberal critics said they feared the original draft could harm Russia's economy and make Lukashenko, who once professed some respect for Adolf Hitler, a key player in Moscow politics.
Above all, liberals feared Lukashenko could win jurisdiction over some decisions affecting Russia under a nine-member Supreme Council set to oversee the Russia-Belarus union under the draft.
The new document "is much more thought-out than before, thanks to intelligent people", Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov told reporters at the Kremlin.

Yeltsin said the "Treaty on a Union of Belarus and Russia" gave citizens of the two countries freedom of movement and rights of residency, property ownership and participation in local elections in both Belarus and Russia.

It also involved big savings on border guarding and defence and would make police work easier. But he said it would not interfere with the constitution of either state and did not for the moment involve monetary union.

"It is entirely in line with those norms which have existed for a long time in the countries of the European Union. Democracy and respect for human rights is one of the bases of our union," Yeltsin said.
"We have a lot of work to do on creating a single currency as mentioned in the draft charter," he said, adding that debates on the charter would be outlined in media broadcasts.

Existing integration efforts with Belarus, which include a separate customs agreement also involving Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, have become mired in problems, with Russian officials accusing Belarus of not playing by the rules.

Economists say that while Belarus offers Russia a strategic corridor to the West for lucrative energy supplies, its backward economy would weigh heavily on Russia, whose own economic transition is fraught with difficulties.
Vladimir Kryuchkov, a former chairman of the KGB who participated in the 1991 coup attempt against Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev, said that he favoured swift integration.
"I'm afraid it will be just paper again," he said. "Only a great Russia can resist and only a great Russia can satisfy the demands of its population," he told a news conference.
